claim: Fatty liver is harmless and needs no treatment.
verdict: Fatty liver can slowly scar the liver.
truth: In some people, fat in the liver causes inflammation that slowly turns into scarring and, over years, cirrhosis. The good news: early fatty liver can be reversed.
do: Losing 7 to 10% of body weight, about 150 minutes of brisk walking a week and cutting out sugary drinks can reverse early fatty liver.
doctor: Ask about a liver stiffness test (FibroScan) if you have fatty liver along with diabetes, extra weight or abnormal liver tests.

verdict: Most people find it far easier than they expected.
truth: An upper endoscopy usually takes 5 to 10 minutes. It is done with a throat spray or light sedation, so there is little or no pain.
do: Come with an empty stomach (6 to 8 hours), bring your old reports, and ask for sedation if you feel anxious.

claim: Only people who drink alcohol get liver disease.
verdict: Many liver diseases have nothing to do with alcohol.
truth: Fatty liver linked to weight and diabetes is now one of the commonest liver problems in India. Hepatitis B and C, some medicines and herbal or 'detox' supplements can also damage the liver.
do: If you have diabetes or carry extra weight around the belly, get a liver function test and an ultrasound. Check with a doctor before starting herbal supplements.

claim: Jaundice clears up on its own with rest and home remedies.
verdict: Jaundice is a sign that needs a cause.
truth: Jaundice can come from hepatitis, a stone blocking the bile duct, medicines or, less often, a growth. Some of these need treatment quickly, and home remedies cannot tell them apart.
do: Get blood tests and an ultrasound to find the cause. Avoid unproven herbal remedies, which can harm the liver further.
doctor: Go to hospital the same day if jaundice comes with fever, confusion, drowsiness or bleeding.

claim: Colon cancer only happens in old age.
verdict: It is being seen more and more in younger adults.
truth: Colon cancer is rising in adults under 50. Found early, it is highly treatable.
do: Don't ignore blood in the stool, a lasting change in bowel habit, unexplained weight loss or anaemia, whatever your age.
doctor: See a gastroenterologist if any of these last more than 2 to 3 weeks.

claim: A glass of cold milk cures acidity.
verdict: Milk soothes for a few minutes, then can make it worse.
truth: Milk coats the food pipe briefly, which feels soothing. But its fat and protein prompt the stomach to make more acid, so the burning often comes back.
do: Eat smaller meals, finish dinner 3 hours before bed, and cut down on fried food, tea and coffee. For occasional heartburn, an antacid works better.
doctor: See a doctor if heartburn happens twice a week or more, or comes with trouble swallowing, vomiting or weight loss.

claim: Black, sticky stools can be a sign of bleeding in the stomach.
verdict: True, and it needs medical care the same day.
truth: Blood from the stomach turns black as it is digested, giving tar-like, sticky, foul-smelling stools. Iron tablets can also darken stools, but those stools are usually firm, not sticky.
do: If your stools turn black and sticky, especially with dizziness or weakness, or if you take painkillers or blood thinners, go to a hospital emergency department.

verdict: Silent gallstones often need no surgery.
truth: Many gallstones are found by chance on an ultrasound and never cause trouble. Surgery is usually advised once stones cause pain or complications such as infection, jaundice or pancreatitis.
do: If your stones cause no symptoms, ask your doctor whether watching them is safe for you. A few people, for example those with very large stones, are still advised surgery.
doctor: Pain in the upper right belly after meals, fever or yellow eyes need a doctor promptly.

verdict: Most loose motions settle without antibiotics.
truth: Most bouts of diarrhoea are caused by viruses, which antibiotics cannot kill. Antibiotics you don't need can upset your gut bacteria and cause side effects.
do: Drink ORS after every loose stool, keep eating light home food, and give it 2 to 3 days.
doctor: See a doctor for blood in the stool, high fever, very little urine or dizziness, or if it lasts more than 3 days. Older people need care sooner.

claim: Hepatitis B spreads by sharing food and utensils.
verdict: It spreads through blood, not food.
truth: Hepatitis B passes through blood and body fluids: from mother to baby at birth, unsafe injections, shared razors, unscreened blood and unprotected sex. It does not spread through food, water, utensils, hugs or coughing.
do: Get a simple HBsAg blood test. If it is negative, three doses of the vaccine give long-lasting protection.
doctor: If the test is positive, see a liver specialist. Most people do well with regular check-ups and, when needed, tablets.
